title: Multicore & Multiprocessing
summary: Why chipmakers stopped chasing clock speed and started stacking cores instead — and why doubling cores rarely doubles performance.

blocks.markdown:
**Multicore** means one chip holds several independent CPU cores instead of one fast core.

- Around the mid-2000s, clock speeds stopped climbing — chips ran too hot to push further.
- The industry's answer: add more cores instead of a faster one.
- More cores only help if the software actually splits work across them.
- This is [instruction-level-parallelism](instruction-level-parallelism) moved up a level — from overlapping instructions to overlapping whole threads.

blocks.subTitle: The power wall
blocks.markdown:
For decades, faster clocks meant faster chips. Then power got in the way.

- Chip power roughly scales with the **cube** of clock speed — small speed gains cost huge extra heat.
- Past ~4 GHz, cooling a single core became impractical for everyday chips.
- Two cores at a lower clock do more total work per watt than one core pushed to its limit.

This is the **power wall**: the reason single-core speed growth stalled.

Three words that get mixed up constantly.

- **Processor (CPU chip)** — the physical package plugged into the socket.
- **Core** — one independent execution unit inside that chip; each can run its own instruction stream.
- **Thread** — a sequence of instructions the OS schedules; many threads can share one core over time.

A laptop can have **1 processor, 8 cores, 16 threads** — that gap between cores and threads is **simultaneous multithreading**, covered next.

**SMP (symmetric multiprocessing)** is the standard multicore setup: every core is identical, sees the **same memory**, and can run any task equally well.

- The OS scheduler treats cores interchangeably — any thread can run on any core.
- "Symmetric" means no core is special or reserved; they're peers.
- Nearly every laptop, phone, and server CPU today is an SMP design.

blocks.subTitle: One core, two threads
blocks.markdown:
**SMT (simultaneous multithreading)**, sold as **hyperthreading** by Intel, lets one physical core present itself as **two logical cores** to the OS.

- The core duplicates cheap state (registers) but keeps one set of execution units.
- When one thread stalls waiting on memory, the core fills the gap with work from the other thread.
- It's not two real cores — expect roughly **20-30% extra throughput**, not 2x.

Why the OS shows more "CPUs" than physical cores.

| | Physical core | SMT / logical thread |
|---|---|---|
| Execution units | Own, dedicated | Shared with sibling |
| Runs in parallel | Always, fully | Only fills stalls |
| Speedup vs real core | 1x baseline | Partial, ~1.2-1.3x |

Task Manager showing "16 CPUs" on an 8-core chip means 8 real cores, 8 SMT threads riding along.

Two different ways to exploit parallelism, at two different levels.

- **ILP (instruction-level parallelism)** — one core overlaps instructions from a *single* thread (pipelining, out-of-order execution). See [instruction-level-parallelism](instruction-level-parallelism).
- **TLP (thread-level parallelism)** — *multiple* threads run at once, across cores or via SMT.

ILP hit diminishing returns first; TLP via multicore is what picked up the slack.

How cores in a parallel system see memory.

| | Shared memory | Distributed memory |
|---|---|---|
| Address space | One, all cores see it | Separate per node |
| Communication | Read/write shared RAM | Explicit messages |
| Typical scale | Single machine (SMP) | Clusters, many machines |

Multicore desktops use shared memory; large server clusters combine both — shared within a machine, distributed across machines.

blocks.subTitle: The intuition
blocks.markdown:
**Amdahl's law**: a program's speedup from parallel cores is capped by the fraction that *can't* be parallelized.

- Split any program into a **serial part** (must run one-at-a-time) and a **parallel part** (splittable across cores).
- No matter how many cores you throw at the parallel part, the serial part still runs at the same speed.
- That serial sliver becomes the hard ceiling on total speedup.

blocks.subTitle: The formula, briefly
blocks.markdown:
If **s** is the serial fraction, max speedup with infinite cores is **1 / s**.

- 10% serial (s = 0.1) → speedup can never exceed **10x**, even with 1000 cores.
- 1% serial → cap is 100x — small serial slivers still bite at large core counts.

The formula: `speedup(N) = 1 / (s + (1-s)/N)`, where N is the number of cores.

Adding cores helps a lot at first, then barely at all.

The curve bends early — most of the missed speedup shows up well before 64 cores.

Beyond the serial fraction, real chips add more friction.

- **Shared resources** — cores compete for shared cache and memory bandwidth; more cores means more contention.
- **Coordination overhead** — locks and synchronization between threads cost time and don't parallelize.
- **Not enough parallel work** — some problems simply don't split into enough independent pieces.

So real speedup curves flatten even faster than Amdahl's law alone predicts.

Common mistakes:

- **"8 cores = 8x speedup."** Only if the whole workload parallelizes perfectly — real code never does.
- **"Hyperthreading doubles a core."** It's one core sharing execution units across two threads, not two real cores.
- **"More cores always help."** Past the point where work runs out or contention dominates, extra cores sit idle or slow things down.

blocks.subTitle: Why multicore
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why did CPUs go multicore instead of just faster?**

Power scales roughly with the cube of clock speed, so pushing a single core past a few GHz became too hot to cool economically. Splitting the chip into multiple lower-clocked cores does more total work per watt — that's the **power wall** forcing the shift from ILP to thread-level parallelism.

blocks.subTitle: Core vs thread
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between a core and a thread?**

A **core** is a physical execution unit — it can genuinely run instructions in parallel with other cores. A **thread** is a schedulable instruction stream; several threads can share one core over time, or run one-per-core. SMT (hyperthreading) blurs this by letting one core expose two logical threads, but the execution hardware is still shared.

blocks.subTitle: What hyperthreading is
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is hyperthreading, exactly?**

Intel's name for SMT: one physical core duplicates lightweight state (registers) so it can hold two threads' contexts at once, but the execution units and caches are still shared. When one thread stalls on a cache miss, the core switches to useful work from the other — a throughput gain, not a doubling of compute.

blocks.subTitle: Amdahl's law
blocks.markdown:
**Q: State Amdahl's law and its implication.**

Speedup with N cores is `1 / (s + (1-s)/N)`, where s is the fraction of the program that must run serially. As N grows toward infinity, speedup caps at `1/s`. Implication: shrinking the serial fraction matters more than adding cores — a program that's 20% serial can never exceed 5x speedup, however many cores you add.

blocks.subTitle: Why not linear speedup
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why don't 4 cores give 4x speedup?**

Three reasons stack up: Amdahl's law caps it at the serial fraction, cores contend for shared cache and memory bandwidth, and synchronization between threads (locks, waiting) adds overhead that doesn't parallelize. Real workloads rarely split into perfectly independent, equal-sized chunks either — so measured speedup is almost always well below linear.
